content: The 74th World Health Assembly, held in Geneva from May 24 to June 1, 2021, adopted several resolutions and decisions aimed at advancing global health initiatives. Among these was Resolution A/RES/75/310, titled Vision for Everyone: Accelerating Action to Achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, which was adopted by the General Assembly on July 23, 2021. This resolution emphasizes the importance of integrating eye care into broader health systems to achieve universal health coverage and sustainable development goals. Efforts to accelerate progress in the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including oral health and integrated eye care, were highlighted in the WHO South-East Asia Region. This includes the development of comprehensive strategies and monitoring frameworks to address these health challenges effectively. The WHO has also developed a Package of Eye Care Interventions to guide countries in implementing evidence-based eye care services. This package includes tools for monitoring progress, such as the Eye Care Indicator Menu (ECIM), which helps track strategies and actions for eye care provision. Financial risk protection for essential eye care services, such as cataract surgery, diabetic retinopathy laser treatment, glaucoma surgeries, and anti-VEGF injections, is a critical component of universal health coverage. Governments are encouraged to provide financial coverage for these services to reduce the economic burden on individuals and improve access to care. The integration of eye care into national health plans and primary health care training is a key strategy for achieving the goals of the WHO’s Integrated People-Centered Eye Care (IPEC) approach. This includes incorporating primary eye care into national training curricula for primary care providers and implementing early detection programs for preschool-aged children to identify and address vision impairments at an early stage. Monitoring indicators, such as the availability of refractive services, waiting times for cataract surgery, and the quality of surgical outcomes, are essential for evaluating the effectiveness of eye care services. Efforts to eliminate trachoma as a public health problem remain a priority, with strategies such as trachomatous trichiasis surgery being made accessible and affordable. The WHO also highlights the importance of vision rehabilitation services for individuals with irreversible vision impairment or blindness. These services aim to optimize functioning in daily life and mitigate the consequences of lost vision. Finally, the WHO underscores the need for robust data collection and reporting systems to map the distribution of eye conditions and monitor the utilization of eye care services. This information is vital for planning and improving eye care delivery, particularly in underserved populations.
